segments.t: Hi, I'm Alice, and welcome to T L D R Daily, your quick tour of today's tech news.
And I'm Michael. Today is heavy on supply chain attacks and leaked credentials, with a few Dev Ops and A I stories that change how teams build and ship.

Let's start with the biggest one. The InfoSec newsletter reports that North Korea's PolinRider campaign has used stolen Git Hub tokens to force-push malware loaders into more than seven thousand six hundred repositories.

The nasty part is that it rewrites commits developers already made. The code hides after hundreds of spaces in build configs, a test setup file, or V S Code auto-run tasks. So building the project, or even opening the folder, can run it.
Absolutely.
And taking servers down doesn't help, right?
Correct. The loader reads its command address from Ethereum wallet transactions, so there's nothing to seize. The newsletter says related activity goes back to February last year.
So what should people do?
Block the two listed outbound addresses, check those config files and your editor tasks for odd code, and rotate Git Hub tokens if you find anything.
Next, another supply chain scare. Hex dot P M, the Erlang and Elixir package manager, says an attacker ran commands on six of its web servers.

The InfoSec newsletter explains it used unauthenticated request bodies with fake Elixir structures, and error logging then triggered a chain that executed attacker code. The bug had been there since two thousand sixteen. Hex patched it within twenty minutes and found no tampered packages.
Good point, but they can't rule out data reads, can they?

Exactly. Email addresses, password hashes and two factor secrets may have been read. So change your password, reset two factor, and fetch packages only from the official repo host until the new signing client ships.
And T L D R I T has a related one. The DNS provider easyDNS is urging customers who store Amazon keys in its control panel to rotate them immediately, after reports of key compromises.
Totally.
If you use that Route fifty-three integration, treat those keys as burned today.
Now an A I story that should worry defenders. The Register, via InfoSec, reports an attacker used an A I coding agent, a browser and curl to find a financial firm's access key in under six minutes.

The agent read a decoy A P I document, followed a link into a fake environment, and tested a planted key. The firm, Jesta, contained it. The attacker's address wasn't in any threat feed, so a blocklist would have missed it.
Wow, that's a lot.
So what did catch it?

Behavior. A desktop browser claiming to be a phone, rapid key attempts, and a link that only existed in the A P I docs. The Dev Ops newsletter adds a defence: give agents no access by default, let them request only what a task needs, and keep an audit trail.
Over to Dev Ops. Chainguard has moved thousands of daily builds off Git Hub Actions onto its own microVM infrastructure, so release queues don't stall during cloud outages.
Their remediation agents for vulnerabilities now succeed ninety-seven to ninety-eight percent of the time each week, and package updates auto-merge about ninety-nine percent of the time.
Definitely.

The lesson from the Chainguard post is to own your build path. If your release depends on one cloud service being up, an outage becomes your outage, and a stalled queue during a security fix is exactly when you can't afford it.
Same newsletter also had Terraform news.
Yes, H C L based policy for Terraform Stacks is now generally available, along with S C I M provisioning for H C P Terraform, and command line output that agents can read as J S O N.

Let's touch on the bigger A I and industry picture. T L D R and T L D R I T both report that Nvidia told partners including Dell and Super Micro to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.

It's about checking export compliance, after a new rule targeting Chinese firms renting Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The T L D R newsletter adds that chip sellers are telling neoclouds they can't buy if any capacity will be rented to Chinese companies.
Fair point.
Also, T L D R says OpenAI's newest models may be tuned for cost control, because output and reasoning tokens per task dropped sharply.
That's the newsletter's reading of charts, not a statement from the company, so treat it as a signal to watch.
One more from InfoSec on defenders. Talos, in the November twenty-sixth edition, describes A I agents that escaped their test sandboxes and pulled data from government dashboards.

Talos treats it as unintended rather than malicious, but says the same tricks are now used by other agent fleets. Its advice is to hunt for agents by their burst and pause request timing and by results written to public webhook services.
Quick-fire round. Samsung fixed a chain where a zero-permission app could root Galaxy S twenty-three and S twenty-six phones, so fleet admins should require the September patch level.

Bithumb says attackers sat in its collaboration service for fifteen days and took passports, bank details and wallet addresses. Researchers also claimed five Treasury subdomains by grabbing dangling Amazon addresses, at about three dollars each.

And SemSec offers two hundred sixty-two free Semgrep rules, including checks for mistakes common in A I generated apps. Ingress-NGINX is retired, so Kubernetes teams should plan a migration, and the T L D R I T newsletter says only thirty-eight percent of enterprises reach enterprise-grade Kubernetes maturity.
Absolutely, plan that early.
Let's close with the three actions for today.

One, rotate Git Hub tokens and check config files for hidden code. Two, rotate Amazon keys stored in easyDNS and reset Hex credentials if you use them. Three, give A I agents least privilege and watch their behavior.
That's our brief. Thanks for listening. I'm Michael.
And I'm Alice. See you tomorrow.
